name: Security Logging and Incident Response
intent: Record the events that let you notice and reconstruct an attack, without recording secrets, then detect, contain and learn from incidents faster than the attacker can use their access.
scenario: One day of failed logins for a service with 23 sources: 20 ordinary users, an office behind one shared address (40 people), a fast attacker guessing passwords for 10 minutes, and a slow one trying one password a minute for five hours. Both get in at the end. A single on-call engineer looks at alerts one by one.
problem: Without good logs you cannot tell what happened, and with bad ones you leak the very secrets you are protecting. Even with logs, a detection rule that is too loose buries the one real alert in false ones, so the on-call person stops trusting it. A rule that is too tight misses the slow attacker completely. And detecting an attack is only half the job: what matters is how long the attacker keeps access, which also depends on how fast someone can act.

howItWorks.title: Log events that answer who, what, when, where and what happened
howItWorks.text: Security-relevant events are sign-ins (success and failure), authorisation denials, privilege and role changes, data exports, admin actions and configuration changes. Each entry needs a timestamp in a synchronised clock, the actor, the target, the source address, the outcome and a request id that ties it to other logs. Structured fields make them searchable.

howItWorks.title: Never log secrets, and keep personal data to what you need
howItWorks.text: Passwords, session tokens, API keys, full card numbers and private keys must not appear in logs, even when a request fails or a debug flag is on. Logs are copied to many systems and read by many people, so a leaked secret there lives for the retention period. Redact or drop sensitive fields at the point where the line is written, mask what you must keep (last four digits), and treat log access as sensitive.

howItWorks.title: Make logs hard to change quietly
howItWorks.text: An attacker who gets onto a host will try to delete or edit its logs. Ship events off the machine as they happen, store them append-only or write-once, and limit who may delete. A hash chain, where each entry includes a hash of the previous one, makes edits detectable, but someone who can rewrite the whole chain can recompute it, so the latest hash must also be kept somewhere they cannot write.

howItWorks.title: Detection rules trade false alarms against misses
howItWorks.text: A rule has a window and a threshold, such as 10 failed logins from one source in 5 minutes. Low thresholds catch more but alert on every typo and on a shared office address after a password reset, which produces alert fatigue. High thresholds stay quiet but miss a patient attacker. A longer window with a higher threshold catches slow attacks. Rules need an owner, a runbook and a regular look at what they actually fired on.

howItWorks.title: Time to detect is not time to contain
howItWorks.text: Detection is the clock until someone knows. Containment is the clock until the attacker can no longer act, and it includes waiting in the alert queue, triage, and doing the thing (blocking a source, revoking a session, rotating a key). A runbook that says exactly what to do cuts the last part. Automatic blocking cuts all of it, but acts on false alarms too and can lock out real users. Afterwards, hold a blameless review: timeline, what worked, what to change.

pros: Good logs turn an incident from guesswork into a timeline
Tuned detection finds attacks while the attacker is still working
Runbooks shorten containment and let any on-call engineer act
Post-incident reviews feed the fixes back into rules, logging and design
cons: Log volume costs money to store, move and search, so retention has to be chosen
Rules need continuous tuning, since traffic and attackers change
Automatic response can harm real users when a rule is wrong
Logs themselves become a sensitive data store that needs protection
whenToUse: Security event logging on every service that authenticates users or holds sensitive data
Rate and correlation alerts on sign-in, privilege changes and data export
A written runbook for each alert that pages a person
whenNotToUse: Logging whole request and response bodies in production 'for debugging'
Automatic blocking on a rule that has not been run in alert-only mode first
Paging a person for alerts that nobody has ever needed to act on
pitfalls: Logging passwords, tokens, keys or full card numbers, often by accident through a request dump or an exception message
Keeping logs only on the host that can be compromised, so the attacker erases them
A hash chain with no copy of the head elsewhere, which an attacker with write access simply recomputes
Thresholds so low that nearly every alert is false, until the real one is ignored
Alerting per source address when many users share one address, so one password reset locks the office out
Measuring only time to detect and forgetting the queue, triage and action before the access ends
Skipping the post-incident review because the incident was embarrassing, so the same gap is still there next time

quiz.question: A login handler logs the whole request when a login fails, to help debug. What is the main security problem?
options: It makes the logs so large that searching them in an incident becomes too slow to use
Failed logins should never be logged at all, because they say nothing useful about attacks
Passwords and tokens end up in log storage, which many people and systems can read and which is kept for months
The timestamps in the log are no longer in order once the request body is added
quiz.explanation: A request dump copies the secret into every system that receives logs, and it stays for the whole retention period. Failed logins are exactly what should be logged, but the secret fields must be redacted when the line is written. Size and ordering are secondary.

quiz.question: A rule fires 30 times a day for 3 failed logins in 5 minutes, nearly all harmless, while a slow attacker makes one attempt per minute. What change helps most?
options: Lower the threshold to 2 failures in 5 minutes so that more attempts are caught
Raise the threshold to 20 failures in the same 5 minutes to remove the noise
Ignore the rule from now on, because most of its alerts are false anyway
Use a longer window, such as 60 minutes, with a higher threshold such as 40
quiz.explanation: A slow attacker never reaches a high count within 5 minutes, but accumulates it over an hour, while ordinary typos do not. Lowering the threshold adds noise, and raising it inside the same window misses the slow attacker entirely. Ignoring the rule gives up detection.

quiz.question: An attacker with admin rights on the log server edits entry 2 and recomputes every later hash in a hash-chained log. What can still reveal the edit?
options: Nothing at all, because the chain is internally consistent after the recomputation
The latest hash, compared with a copy kept in a store the attacker cannot write to
The chain itself, because every hash depends on the hash of the entry before it
The file size on disk, which always changes whenever any single entry is edited
quiz.explanation: Recomputing the chain makes it self-consistent, so the chain alone cannot expose the edit. A head hash kept elsewhere (write-once storage, another system) no longer matches. File size is not reliable evidence.
